title: Follow me (Mark 1:14–20)
hookLine: Mark's favorite word: immediately they left their nets

cards: Early morning on the Sea of Galilee. It's really a lake, and the fishing is hard work: nets, boats, cold water, a family business. Two brothers, Simon and Andrew, stand in the shallows casting a net.

A man walks along the shore. He stops, looks at them, and says two words, more or less: follow me. Down the beach, it happens again, with two more brothers, James and John, mending nets in their father's boat.
The opposite of what they do is familiar: meant to, planned to, will get to it. And Mark's word for what they did is the heartbeat of his whole gospel.

teach.b: Immediately. In Greek, euthys. Mark uses it again and again; read him in one sitting and it's everywhere.
The King James Bible often says straightway. Once you notice it, you can't stop: straightway he saw the heavens torn, immediately the Spirit drove him out, and now this. First, the scene.
John the Baptist has been arrested.

Jesus comes into Galilee announcing: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel." Repent, in Mark's Greek, is about a change of mind, a new direction. Then the lake.
He sees Simon and Andrew casting a net, and says: "Come ye after me, and I will make you to become fishers of men." A fisherman's joke, almost: you catch fish now, you'll catch people.
"And straightway they forsook their nets, and followed him." No negotiation, no three-month notice. A little further on, James and John are in their boat with their father, Zebedee.

Jesus calls them, and they leave their father in the boat with the hired men, and go. Mark doesn't say what they were thinking, or whether they'd met Jesus before; John's gospel suggests some of them had.

teach.h: A FATHER LEFT IN THE BOAT.
teach.b: Readers notice the cost, too: a father left sitting in a boat.

For Mark, immediately is not recklessness. It's the rhythm of a story where God's time has arrived and can't wait. Some readers hear it as a question: what's the net in my hands, and what would it mean to put it down?

how: Many Christians read the calling of the first disciples as a call to their own lives, and churches often read it when commissioning people for new work or ministry.

o: slowly, once the timing finally feels right
at once, with no stalling: Mark's heartbeat word
after careful thought and planning ahead

games.q: you're Simon, casting a net at dawn. a man on the shore says: come after me, and I'll make you fishers of men. what do you do?
o: leave the nets immediately and follow.
ask for time to talk it over with your family.
games.why: "and straightway they forsook their nets, and followed him." Mark's word, at the moment it matters.

practice: Think of one small, good thing you've been putting off: texting a friend who's struggling, apologizing, signing up to help, returning the call, opening the Bible you meant to open.
Notice the net in your hands, the reasons, the timing, the someday, and picture putting it down and doing the thing. If you pray, you can ask for the nerve to do it today.
